extracted.intended_audience: aspiring microfiction / flash fiction writers (contest entrants, creative-writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for composing compelling microfiction (stories of 100 words or less) that contain a complete emotional arc, clear structure, tense stakes, precise diction, and rounded characters. Advice focuses on hooks, word-level choices, revision, and exercises for getting started.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start with a hook
rubrics_metrics.description: Start your story without preamble, with your protagonist acting, doing, or thinking something that’s not only interesting, but something meaningful. Many successful shorts start not only in Media Res (in the middle of a narrative), but in a moment of conflict/tension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use your opening sentence not only to grab attention, but to tease/reveal stakes. Your opening sentence isn’t your only hook — use the title to snag attention and (better yet) set/tease your story’s tone/mood. Begin where it matters: in a moment of conflict or tension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make every word matter (exact diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Utilize exact diction: consider not only the standard meaning of each word, but the tone, sonority (sound and the shape/feel of a spoken word), and the emotional resonance evoked through your word choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use word choice to impact speed/pace (shorter words = a faster read). Prefer words with layered meanings to add complexity/nuance. Consider how diction can be used to raise tension/stakes and to reveal character or tone in very few words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have a clear beginning, middle, and end — AND a full emotional arc
rubrics_metrics.description: Great microfiction is a complete, complex story despite its brevity: a clear beginning, middle, and end plus a full emotional arc. This doesn't require the character to undergo an explicit emotional change, but it does require taking the reader through an emotional shift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give readers a surprise twist; invite empathy and deliver an emotional sucker punch. Ask how your story can imbue meaning or invite readers to experience/explore a certain idea or emotion. If stuck, write longer drafts and then edit down to find the heart of the story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rising tension/stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Microfiction should include rising tension or stakes so the short arc feels earned and compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tease or reveal stakes early (the opening sentence is a place to do this). Use conflict/tension from the start and employ diction and pacing to escalate stakes across the piece even within very few words.

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft round (nuanced) characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should feel rounded and nuanced even in miniature form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep it simple: focus on fewer characters (1–2) and a single problem or a very specific question/theme. Use specific details that invite emotional experience. Employ poetic elements (meter, rhyme, alliteration, personification, rhythm, etc.) to convey meaning and emotion economically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin in media res / begin where it matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Start in the middle of things and in a moment of conflict/tension rather than with preamble or setup.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Opening with action/thought that matters reveals character and stakes simultaneously; it helps hook the reader immediately and leaves less need for exposition in a 100-word piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revision strategy: write longer, then edit shorter
rubrics_metrics.description: Finding the emotional core of a microfiction often requires multiple drafts; start with a longer draft to discover the heart, then cut ruthlessly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing longer then editing shorter helps you learn what to keep and what to cut. Microfiction forces attention to internal/external arcs, pacing, and characterization — use edits to distill each sentence's contribution to those elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use microfiction as a craft tool (exercises & applications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Microfiction can be used beyond standalone pieces — as a pre-plotting device for novels or as a revision tool to test emotional beats and chapter impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Try exercises to generate material: pick a character/emotion/problem and write a six-word story, then expand; pick a visible object, imagine who last used it, and turn that event into a story with a surprise twist. Use micro scenes to determine content, order, and emotional impact for larger works.
